# Development and Evaluation of a Planetary Health Diet Index: The Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America Study

**Authors:** Nilendra K. Nair; Linh P. Bui; Caleigh M. Sawicki; Namratha R. Kandula; Alka M. Kanaya; Kyu Ha Lee; Meir Stampfer; Walter C. Willett; Shilpa N. Bhupathiraju

Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA. C. M. Sawicki is a postdoctoral researcher, Channing Division of Network Medicine, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA. N. ## Abstract

In 2019, the EAT-Lancet Commission introduced the Planetary Health Diet (PHD), aiming to enhance both human health and global environmental sustainability. Although a few indexes have been developed based on the PHD for different populations, there is currently no index tailored specifically for the South Asian population.

This study aimed to develop and validate a Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) based on the EAT-Lancet PHD in a prospective South Asian cohort based in the United States.

Analysis was conducted using cross-sectional dietary data obtained from a validated, ethnic-specific semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire administered to adults in the Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America study at a baseline visit between 2010 and 2013.

A total of 906 participants were enrolled at baseline, recruited from Chicago and the San Francisco Bay Area, in this community-based prospective cohort. Eligible participants were individuals of South Asian ancestry (defined as having 3 or more grandparents born in India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, or Sri Lanka) with no history of cardiovascular disease, aged between 40 and 84 years, and proficient in English, Urdu, or Hindi. The analytic sample included a total of 891 participants without missing data or implausible energy intakes.

The main outcome measure was the PHDI score and its associations with assessments of construct validity and internal reliability.

Linear regression models were used to examine the construct validity of the PHDI, as well as correlations between the index and the Alternative Healthy Eating Index and the dietary carbon footprint. Analysis of variance was used to evaluate the concurrent-criterion validity and principal components analysis to assess multidimensionality. Pearson correlations were estimated between the PHDI components and energy, and Cronbach’s coefficient α was determined to assess internal consistency.

The PHDI was composed of 15 food components with intake ranges as prescribed by the 2019 EAT-Lancet PHD and scored proportionally 0 to 10 for a total possible score between 0 and 140. PHDI scores ranged from 51 to 119 out of 140 possible points, with a mean score of 89. PHDI was positively associated with plant-derived nutrients such as vegetable protein (P < .0001), total fiber (P < .0001), vitamins A (P < .006) and C (P < .012), and negatively associated with animal-sourced nutrients such as animal protein, cholesterol, and vitamin B12 (P < .0001 for all), amongst others. Concurrent criteria validity revealed significant differences among subgroups: current smokers scored lower (85) than nonsmokers (89) (P = .03); those with bachelor’s degrees scored higher (89.3) than those without (85.4) (P < .0001); higher family income correlated with higher scores (89.7 vs 86.7; P < .0001); and participants with type 2 diabetes had higher scores (90.8) than those with prediabetes (88) (P = .002) or normal glycemia (88.4) (P < .008). Each 5-unit increase in PHDI score was associated with a higher Alternative Healthy Eating Index score (partial correlation: r = 0.7; P < .0001) and a 7% lower dietary carbon footprint (P < .001). Cronbach’s α for internal reliability was .68.

The findings provided support for both the construct validity and reliability of the PHDI in this cohort of American South Asians. This index is suitable for assessing diets in relation to the 2019 EAT-Lancet dietary guidelines.

CLIMATE CHANGE IS A CRITICAL ISSUE IN THE world today, with human habits of production and consumption contributing heavily to its acceleration.1 The current food production system is a major driver of the global syndemic of anthropogenic climate change and malnutrition.2 Diet is linked to climate change through a complex set of interactions that involve both the production and consumption of food.2,3 According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the food system contributes to 25% to 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions, encompassing emissions from livestock production, fertilizer use, and land-use change.4-7 Expansion of agricultural land due to rising food demand drives deforestation, releasing stored carbon and diminishing forests’ carbon-absorbing capacity.8-10

The ubiquity and demand for Westernized diets rich in animal-sourced foods have exacerbated land degradation, air and water pollution, and a global rise in diet-related noncommunicable diseases.2,11 Transitioning to sustainable, more plant-based diets could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 41% to 74%, benefiting both health and climate resilience, and thereby reducing climate-induced illnesses and mortality.4,12,13 Recognizing this need, the EAT-Lancet Commission on Healthy Diets from Sustainable Food Systems proposed a healthy dietary pattern in 2019 that also incorporated sustainability considerations.14 Developed by an international scientific commission of 37 experts, the reference diet is based on a scientific evaluation of the health implications of consuming specific food groups, reductions in food loss and waste, as well as improved agricultural practices that were determined to be environmentally sustainable. This dietary pattern emphasizes the consumption of whole plant-based foods, fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and whole grains, while encouraging limited consumption of red and processed meats, dairy products, added sugars, and refined grains.14 The EAT-Lancet Healthy Diet provides a benchmark for thinking about nutrition and health on a global scale, offering insight into the environmental impacts of our food choices, and presenting a pathway for promoting sustainability and healthy diets.

Developing a diet quality metric to reflect adherence to the EAT-Lancet reference diet is important not only for investigating health outcomes but can also be used as an informational tool for lowering an individual’s carbon footprint. Sustainability was left out of the 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA),15 leaving a void of information that would be of interest to many consumers. Indexes with varying scoring mechanisms based on the EAT-Lancet reference diet have been developed and studied in the context of a few local food cultures, for example, in the Italian,16,17 Brazilian,18 and Danish populations.19 However, an index tailored to the unique dietary habits of the South Asian population has yet to be developed.

To fill this important research gap, we used data from a cohort of Americans of South Asian descent who took part in the Mediators of Atherosclerosis among South Asians Living in America (MASALA) study to develop and validate a Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) that quantifies adherence to the EAT-Lancet reference diet.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Setting

The MASALA study is a community-based prospective cohort of self-identified South Asians recruited from Chicago and the San Francisco Bay Area that was established to understand the etiology and prognostic significance of subclinical atherosclerosis.20 Detailed descriptions of the eligibility criteria, recruitment methods, and study measures have been published elsewhere.20 Briefly, eligibility criteria included participants who were of South Asian ancestry (having 3 or more grandparents born in either India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, or Sri Lanka) and had no history of cardiovascular disease; were between ages 40 and 84 years; and possessed the ability to speak and read in English, Urdu, or Hindi.20 Eligible participants were invited for an onsite, 6-hour baseline examination at the University of California, San Francisco, or Northwestern University clinical centers between 2010 and 2013. A total of 906 participants were enrolled at the baseline visit. All participants provided written formal study consent, and the MASALA study protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the University of California, San Francisco, and Northwestern University. The current analysis protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Board of Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA.

### Questionnaires

At the baseline visit, participants visited the clinical field centers where trained bilingual research staff obtained written informed consent. Information on participants’ contacts, demographic data, language use, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, medical conditions, access to medical care, family history of cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes, reproductive history (women only), and current prescription and nonprescription medication and supplement use, including Ayurvedic and other herbal medications, was assessed using questionnaires by the research staff. A traditional cultural beliefs scale consisting of 7 items was specifically developed for the MASALA cohort to assess the sum of traditional cultural measures. These items were scored on a Likert scale, where higher scores indicated weaker adherence to traditional South Asian beliefs.21,22

### Measurement of Diet

Usual dietary intakes over the past 12 months were assessed using an ethnic-specific, validated, semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) designed for participants from South Asia.20,23,24 The FFQ is composed of 163 items, including 61 items unique to the South Asian diet. The daily servings consumed for each item were calculated from the frequency (day, week, month, year, never) and the serving size (average, small, large). The average serving size of each item was provided, whereby a small serving size was defined as half of the average serving size, while a large serving size was 1.5 times the average. The nutrient profile for the FFQ food items has been previously described in detail.20,23,25 Briefly, the Food Processor program (version 6.11)26 was used for standard FFQ food items, whereas nutrient compositions for the 61 unique South Asian FFQ items were derived from South Asian study participants’ recipes.23 Prototype recipes were formed by combining similar dish recipes, and the nutrient composition of each prototype was assigned to its corresponding FFQ item, based on a medium serving size.23,25 Consistent with previous research,25,27 individuals with energy intake deemed implausible, falling below 800 kcal/day or exceeding 4000 kcal/day for men, or below 500 kcal/day or above 3500 kcal/day for women, were excluded (n = 13). We also excluded participants with missing data (n = 2). The analytic sample included a total of 891 participants.

### Development of the PHDI

The PHDI is premised on 15 food groups as previously outlined,28,29 with possible ranges of consumption (in grams per day and kilocalories per day), for an intake of 2500 kcal/day, aligning with the EAT-Lancet reference diet.13 Although we retained the original scoring structure for comparability, we adapted the index by modifying food group classifications to reflect South Asian-specific items not represented in the EAT-Lancet recommendations. These adaptations, such as disaggregating composite dishes and classifying regionally relevant fats and sweeteners, are detailed in Figure 1 (available at www.jandonline.org).

Due to varying local food availability and individual preferences across populations, and recognizing that the optimal intake of 1 food group often relates to the intake levels of others, the aim was to design a flexible overall dietary pattern. Therefore, alongside setting specific targets for each food group, a range of possible intake levels was provided that permits exchanges while maintaining a consistent total energy intake.28 The 163 food items on the FFQ were categorized into the 15 PHDI food groups based on both the EAT-Lancet recommendations and similarities in nutrient content and culinary usage within the South Asian diet. To convert food groups in serving sizes to gram equivalents, we used the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) FoodData Central database30 where available. Composite dishes and dishes unique to South Asian cuisine were first disaggregated using the MyPyramid Equivalents Database 2.0 31 or published literature on the composition of these dishes.32 Disaggregated food groups were then converted to their gram equivalents using the USDA FoodData Central database.30 Figure 1 (available at www.jandonline.org) provides the groupings made for the FFQ.

The whole grain scoring thresholds for the PHDI were informed by the EAT-Lancet diet recommendations, which define reference dietary intake levels based on a 2500 kcal/day model. The PHDI assigns a maximum score of 10 for whole grain intake at 90 g/day for men and 75 g/day for women. Although the DGA does not explicitly prescribe sex-specific recommendations for intake of whole grains, the slightly lower threshold applied for women (75 g/day) in our analysis reflects expected differences in total energy intake between sexes, primarily driven by differences in body weight and activity levels.33 This decision is also consistent with global consumption patterns, which indicate low average intake of whole grains (~38.4 g/day globally in 2010) with substantial international variation ranging between 1.3 g/day to 334.3 g/day across 187 countries.34 Epidemiological studies further support this threshold, demonstrating a plateau in health benefits at approximately 90 g/day,35 whereas excessive carbohydrate intake exceeding 60% of total energy has been associated with increased mortality and impaired micronutrient absorption.36-38 Thus, our selected thresholds maintain consistency with prior applications of the PHDI and facilitate comparability across studies. The scoring criteria are outlined in Table 1. Each of the 15 food groups is assigned a proportional score on a scale of 0 to 10, and intake ranges for each food group were set to be within the limits set forth by the EAT-Lancet reference diet.14,28 The minimum score threshold represents the intake level at which the food group has the least positive influence on both health and the environment, while the maximum score threshold represents the level at which the food group has the highest level of favorable health and environmental impacts.28 The specific thresholds for the minimum and maximum scores vary depending on whether the relationship between each food group and health outcomes is positive or negative. Increased intake falling within recommended consumption ranges of whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts, seafood, legumes, soy products, and unsaturated fats contributed to higher scores among the 15 PHDI food groups. On the other hand, higher scores were assigned to a limited intake of tubers, red/processed meats, poultry, eggs, dairy, saturated fats, and added sugar. For instance, for vegetables, recognized as a healthy food group, the minimum score is 0, indicating no consumption (0 g/day), whereas the maximum score is 10, reflecting a daily intake of 2 to 3 c or more as recommended by the current DGA.15 Conversely, for beef/red meat, an animal-based food that should be limited, an individual receives a score of 0 for daily consumption of 100 g or more but earns a score of 10 for consuming less than or equal to 14 g/day, aligning with the EAT-Lancet target.14 For intakes between the minimum and maximum range, scores were assigned proportionally using linear interpolation. For example, the scoring criteria for whole fruit (a recommended food group) assigns a score of 0 if no fruit is consumed (0 g/day) and a score of 10 if consumption meets or exceeds 200 g/day. If an individual consumes 150 g/day, their score is calculated proportionally as: [(150-0) / (200 — 0) × 10] = 7.5. Similarly, for red and processed meat (a discouraged food group), a score of 0 is assigned for intake at or above 100 g/day, whereas a score of 10 is assigned for intake at or below 14 g/day. A person consuming 20 g/day would receive a score of: [(100-20) / (100 — 14) × 10 ] = 9.30. A higher score indicates a consumption closer to the Planetary Health Diet recommendations. No further deduction or additional score was allocated for consumption out of the suggested range of the 15 food components. Scores for each group were summed for a total of 140 possible points.

### Statistical Analysis

#### PHDI Validity and Reliability.

Summary statistics for PHDI components are presented using both mean ± SD and median (IQR) to account for nonnormal distributions where applicable. To confirm the construct validity of the PHDI, correlations between the total PHDI score, modeled as a continuous variable, and specific nutrients were examined using linear regression models that adjusted for age, sex, and total energy intake. In addition, the concurrent-criterion validity of PHDI was evaluated by utilizing analysis of variance to examine differences in average PHDI scores among groups with known variations in diet quality. To assess the multidimensionality of the PHDI; that is, whether the systematic variation in the observed data is better accounted for by a combination of components rather than driven by a single component, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed. To evaluate whether the PHDI captures diet quality, regression models and partial correlations between the Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI) that was previously calculated for this cohort,39,40 and the PHDI adjusted for age, sex, and total energy intake were examined. To comprehensively evaluate agreement between the PHDI and the AHEI, we performed additional statistical analyses beyond correlation coefficients. Bland-Altman analysis was conducted to assess mean agreement (bias) and limits of agreement between the continuous scores of the 2 indexes. Cohen κ was calculated to assess categorical agreement based on quartiles of the 2 indexes, and Kendall τ was used to evaluate rank-based (ordinal) agreement. Collectively, these analyses provide a robust evaluation of the agreement between the PHDI and the AHEI. Finally, the internal consistency of the PHDI was assessed using Cronbach’s coefficient α41 for the PHDI components. To further evaluate the robustness of internal reliability, we also conducted a leave-1-out Cronbach’s α analysis, in which each PHDI component was sequentially removed to assess its individual influence on the overall α value. Pearson’s correlation between the individual PHDI components was also evaluated.

### Environmental Footprint

To evaluate the dietary carbon equivalent footprint of each person’s diet based on their FFQ data, the greenhouse gas emission (GHGE) metric was computed using the Food Recall Impacts on the Environment for Nutrition and Dietary Studies (dataFRIENDS) database, described elsewhere.42,43 Briefly, dataFRIENDS is premised on an extensive review of the food-based lifecycle assessment literature from 2005 to 2016 and includes GHGE per kilogram for more than 300 foods in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. The dataFRIENDS database subsequently linked these environmental impact values to the USDA food database, providing the kilogram carbon dioxide-equivalent per 100 g of food. This environmental data represents generic “average” influence factors for the production of food consumed in the United States.42,44 For composite dishes and dishes unique to the South Asian population that were unavailable in the USDA database, standardized recipes were used to disaggregate the food components, which were then mapped to the USDA database.32,45,46 The average GHGE per person was estimated by summing the carbon dioxide equivalent from the foods consumed by the individual and standardized to a total daily energy intake of 2500 kcal.42,47 To estimate associations between the PHDI and dietary carbon footprint, participants were first categorized into quartiles of the PHDI score. General linear models were subsequently applied with the standardized carbon dioxide equivalent as the dependent variable and quartiles of PHDI score and total energy intake as independent variables to estimate the energy-adjusted mean GHGE in each quartile of the PHDI.

## RESULTS

The PHDI components and total score developed in the MASALA study are presented in Table 2. The total PHDI score was normally distributed with a mean of 89 points (95% CI, 88 to 90) (Figure 2, available at www.jandonline.org). The score ranged from a low of 51 to a maximum of 119 out of 140 possible points. Participants received the highest mean scores for intakes of poultry (9.45 ± 1.67), red and processed meat (9.42 ± 1.67), eggs (9.34 ± 1.49), vegetables (9.21 ± 1.64), tubers (9.04 ± 2.08), and fruit (8.44 ± 2.53). On average, participants received the lowest scores for intakes of soy (0.78 ± 1.27), legumes (1.09 ± 1.18), nuts (2.78 ± 2.03), fish (2.84 ± 3.71), and unsaturated fats (3.03 ± 2.47).

### PHDI Validity and Reliability

The validity of the PHDI scoring design was evaluated by examining the relationship between the total PHDI score and the intake of specific nutrients from the total diet (Table 3). For each 5-unit increase in the PHDI, intakes were lower for both animal protein (β = −2.5 g; 95% CI, −3.0 to 2.1) and animal-derived nutrients (cholesterol [β = −10.57 mg; 95% CI, −13 to −7.8], vitamin B2 [β = −.05 mg; 95% CI, −0.07 to −0.03], vitamin B12 [−.12 μg; 95% CI, −0.18 to −0.07], and total fat [β = −0.79 g; 95% CI, −1.5 to −0.12]). On the other hand, for each 5-unit increase in the PHDI, intakes were higher for total fiber (β = .7 g; 95% CI, 0.46 to 0.94), vegetable protein (β = 1.11 g; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.50), polyunsaturated fatty acids (β = .25 g; 95% CI, 0.09 to 0.42), vitamin A (β = 44.4 retinol equivalents; 95% CI, 12.8 to 76), vitamin B3 (β = .17 mg; 95% CI, 0.03 to 0.31), vitamin C (β = 3.86 mg; 95% CI, 0.85 to 6.87), vitamin E (β = .08 mg; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.16), folate (β = 7.57 μg; 95% CI, 2.81 to 12.3), iron (β = .33 mg; 95% CI, 0.17 to 0.49), selenium (β = 1.02 μg; 95% CI, 0.78 to 1.25), and chromium (β = .29 μg; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.51) (all P values < .05).

For concurrent-criterion validity, no differences were found in average PHDI scores between men (88.2 ± 0.44) and women (89.5 ± 0.46) (Table 4). However, individuals who were current smokers (85 ± 1.8) had a lower mean PHDI score compared with those who were nonsmokers (89 ± 0.32; P = .03). On average, participants who were aged 50 to 59 years (90 ± 0.54) and 60 to 69 years (90 ± 0.62) had higher PHDI scores than participants who were 40 to 49 years old (87.4 ± 0.55) or 70 to 89 years old (86.4 ± 1.1). Those with bachelor’s degrees had a higher average PHDI score (89.3 ± 0.34) compared with those without (85.4 ± 0.90) (P < .001). Likewise, individuals who reported a family income >$75 000 had significantly higher mean PHDI scores (89.7 ± 0.37) compared with participants whose family income was ≤$75 000 (86.7 ± 0.62) (P < .001). Participants with type 2 diabetes had higher PHDI scores (90.8 ± 0.63) compared with those with prediabetes (88 ± 0.55) (P = .002) or normal glycemia (88.4 ± 0.49) (P < .008). Post hoc pairwise comparisons for variables with more than 2 levels were conducted using the Tukey method to adjust for multiple comparisons; full P values are reported in Table 5 (available at www.jandonline.org) Evaluation of construct validity using the scree plot from the PCA indicated that no single linear combination of PHDI components accounted for a majority of the variance in the data (Figure 3). There was evidence for at least 5 dimensions as 5 factors have eigenvalues >1, indicating each of the 5 principal components explains more variance than a single variable.

In our regression models, after adjusting for age, sex, and total energy, the total PHDI score was significantly and positively associated with the overall diet quality as assessed by the AHEI. Each 5-unit higher PHDI score was associated (β ± SE) with a higher AHEI score (2.39 ± 0.09 units; P < .001 and partial correlation: r = 0.7; P < .0001). In addition, the Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean difference of 18.68 (95% limits of agreement = 4.73 to 32.62), indicating that while the indexes are related, they differ systematically in their absolute scores (Figure 4). Kendall τ (τ = 0.57; P < .001) indicates a statistically significant moderate monotonic relationship between the 2 indexes. Cohen κ (κ = 0.31; P < .001), calculated using the centiles of the indexes, suggests fair agreement. The discrepancy between the higher ordinal association (τ) and lower categorical agreement (κ) may be due to information loss when converting continuous scores into centiles for analysis using Cohen κ. These findings indicate substantial but not perfect agreement between the PHDI and the AHEI.

When correlations between the total PHDI score and its components were examined, the strongest correlation was between total PHDI and the component score for added sugar (r = 0.54; P < .001). On the other hand, whole grains (r = 0.17) and eggs (r = 0.17) had the lowest correlations with PHDI (P < .001). When examining correlations between the individual components, vegetables, and unsaturated fat (r = 0.33), red meat and poultry (r = 0.45), and saturated fat and added sugar (r = 0.45) were strongly correlated with each other. At the same time, both red meat and poultry were inversely correlated with fish intake (r =−0.31) (Figure 5). The overall standardized Cronbach’s α for the PHDI was .68, indicating moderate internal reliability. The leave-1-out Cronbach’s α analysis, performed to evaluate the stability of internal consistency, showed that removing individual components resulted in α values ranging from .61 to .68, with slightly higher α values observed upon removal of fish (α = .68) and whole grains (α = .67) (Table 6, available at www.jandonline.org).

The PHDI had a lower dietary carbon footprint such that participants in the highest vs lowest quartile of the PHDI score had a 21% lower mean dietary carbon footprint (Figure 6). In addition, a 5-unit higher PHDI score was associated with 7% lower dietary carbon footprint (P < .001).

## DISCUSSION

This study developed and evaluated the validity and reliability of a PHDI in a South Asian population that quantifies adherence to the dietary recommendations of the 2019 EAT-Lancet Planetary Health reference diet.14 Utilizing established methods for the validation of a dietary index,48,49 the psychometric analyses of the PHDI demonstrated strong content and construct validity as well as internal reliability. The outcomes of the construct validity analysis were consistent with the findings from previous evaluations of the nutrient profiles in both vegetarian and nonvegetarian dietary patterns.50 The associations in the anticipated direction support the PHDI’s capacity to differentiate between food components per the EAT-Lancet dietary recommendations.

The PHDI discerned significant differences in dietary quality among groups known to have variations in diet quality, revealing noteworthy differences in average PHDI scores. Unlike other studies,51 there was no difference in the diet quality between men and women as assessed by the PHDI. The relationship between smoking status and diet quality has been highlighted by numerous studies, which have shown that current smokers typically have poorer diet quality52 characterized by a preference for energy-dense foods,53 insufficient fruit and vegetable consumption, and high saturated fat intake.54 Our findings also align with prior research in supporting an age-related association with diet quality. Although diet quality generally improves with age for adults aged between 30 to 60 years, the determinants of sustaining healthy eating behaviors in older adults aged 69 years and older are intricate, influenced by factors such as socioeconomic disparities, social isolation, limited education on diet-disease relationships, and the challenges of aging, collectively contributing to declining diet quality among older adults.55,56 Likewise, disparities in diet quality based on income and educational levels have grown over the past decade, and research consistently shows that higher income and education are linked to healthier dietary habits.57,58 Notably, the MASALA study participants overall had high family income and educational achievements,59 which are closely intertwined and may jointly influence individuals’ dietary decisions.

Intriguingly, the relationship between diabetes status and diet quality revealed that individuals diagnosed with diabetes had higher average PHDI scores than those with prediabetes or without diabetes. This could be attributed to reverse causation, wherein postdiagnosis improvements in lifestyle factors prompt individuals to make healthier dietary choices.60,61 Congruent with our findings, the Cardiometabolic Risk Reduction in South Asia (CARRS) study on South Asians also noted this reverse causality, indicating that South Asian adults in urban areas were adjusting their diets after being diagnosed with a disease.62

The PHDI and AHEI scores have several design parallels, encompassing common food groups such as vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and red/processed meats, employing a similar scoring range from 0 to 10 for these food components.40 Capitalizing on these shared attributes, it was anticipated that the PHDI’s assessment of diet quality would demonstrate robust positive correlations with the AHEI score in the MASALA Study. Although both the AHEI and the PHDI aim to assess the quality of dietary patterns, the AHEI focuses primarily on health-related outcomes, considering factors associated with chronic diseases.40 On the other hand, the PHDI has a broader scope, aiming to enhance both health and environmental sustainability.14 It uniquely combines a focus on individual health promotion with an emphasis on mitigating the environmental impact of dietary choices, aligning with the broader concept of planetary health.14,63 Although the PHDI and AHEI showed moderate correlation, Bland-Altman analysis suggested proportional bias across adherence levels, with PHDI tending to overestimate diet quality at higher adherence levels and underestimate it at lower adherence levels. This pattern is a recognized challenge in the validation of self-reported diet quality measures and likely reflects differences in conceptual emphasis between indexes.64 Moreover, because this is a cross-sectional validation within a specific cohort, future research should examine PHDI performance longitudinally and in more diverse populations. These findings underscore the complexity of validating multidimensional dietary indexes and the need to use multiple complementary approaches to assess agreement.

Given that the 2019 EAT-Lancet reference diet promotes a planetary health diet with sustainable environmental impact,14 it was important to also determine the dietary carbon footprint of foods consumed by participants in a South Asian cohort based in the United States. Our findings align with previous research, indicating that diets that favor plant-based foods are associated with lower carbon footprints compared to other prevalent American dietary patterns.43 Furthermore, opting for diets rich in fruits, vegetables, and legumes while reducing the consumption of red and processed meats, especially those from ruminant animals, represents a practical approach for individuals to decrease their carbon footprint resulting from food production.65

The test for internal consistency using the standardized Cronbach’s coefficient α was determined to be .68. As reported by numerous studies, dietary indexes are inherently complex, multidimensional instruments, and expecting individuals to meet all dietary standards consistently is unrealistic.48,49,66,67 Therefore, given that the PCA results indicated that the PHDI was indeed multidimensional, coupled with the rather homogenous cohort of mostly Asian Indian immigrants comprising the MASALA study, the coefficient α value was expected to be lower than the recommended cutoff of .70.41,49 To further assess the stability of the index, results from the leave-1-out Cronbach’s α analysis indicate that no single component had a disproportionate influence on the overall internal consistency of the PHDI. In addition, the low to moderate correlations of the component scores with the total score underscored the reliability. The food groups composed of fruits, nuts, saturated fat, and added sugar seemed to have more influence on the total PHDI score relative to the other components, having correlations ≥.35. Although the lower correlated components might not be adding as much information to the total score, it should be noted that these components might be providing important, independent information.48

Multiple indexes that quantify the 2019 EAT-Lancet Reference Diet have been developed in other populations, each with different approaches and assumptions, and differ significantly from the index developed in this study for South Asians. The index created in the Oxford cohort of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC-Oxford) study considered 14 food groups and used a binary point allocation for a maximum of 14 points.68 However, as previously critiqued,69 this index failed to consider the range of consumption for various food items as prescribed by the EAT-Lancet reference diet. Similarly, the EAT-Lancet index developed in the Swedish Malmö Diet and Cancer cohort70 also considered 14 food groups but scored them differently. It lacked a category for saturated fat and divided the scoring based on consumption categories. The dietary index developed in The Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Adult Health (ELSA-Brasil) cohort18 included 16 food components, resulting in a possible total score ranging from 0 to 150 points. Notably, this index categorized coconut milk and coconut pulp in the nuts food group. However, it is worth mentioning that there is a growing consensus in the field that coconuts should be excluded from the nuts category for nutrition research due to their high saturated fat content,71 which can negatively influence cardiometabolic health.72-74 The PHDI constructed in our study was based on the grams per day consumption of the 15 food groups for a daily intake of 2500 kcal, with coconut categorized under saturated fats due to its high saturated fat content and prevalence in South Asian cuisine.

### Strengths and Limitations

Strengths of our study include that the PHDI developed in the MASALA Study closely aligned with the recommendations from the 2019 EAT-Lancet Commission’s reference diet. Following good practice for a priori dietary indexes,75 the scoring system considered empirical evidence for the associations of the 15 PHDI food groups with health and disease outcomes, as well as the prescribed range of consumption set forth by the reference diet. In addition, the PHDI also proportionally assigned individual scores for the range between minimum and maximum values for the respective food groups. Unique to our approach is the determination of a dietary carbon footprint for individuals of South Asian ancestry living in the United States, which is not only novel but further corroborates the 2019 EAT-Lancet Commission’s dietary recommendations as it relates to beneficial environmental impacts.

This study was not without limitations. Firstly, in our attempts to disaggregate food items unique to the South Asian diaspora and convert them to appropriate gram equivalents from the serving sizes listed in the FFQ, we acknowledge the loss of precision. However, using the USDA database30 in conjunction with conversion factors previously published for this population24,27 aided with the accuracy and consistency of the estimations and, by extension, the classification of the disaggregated items into their appropriate component categories and respective weights in grams per day. With the exception of whole grains, this study applies preexisting dietary PHDI scoring methodology from our group28,29 that uses standardized intake thresholds without explicit sex- or age-specific adjustments.28,29 Although the PHDI framework provides a validated structure for evaluating dietary patterns aligned with planetary health, it does not directly incorporate individualized recommendations for food groups from guidelines such as the DGA.15 Although we applied the original PHDI to facilitate comparability with prior research, this approach inherently constrains flexibility in precisely capturing sex-specific differences in recommended food intake. Future adaptations of the PHDI could consider more nuanced refinements that incorporate sex- and age-specific dietary guidelines explicitly, potentially improving sensitivity and specificity of dietary assessment in diverse populations. Nonetheless, maintaining consistency with previously published scoring methodologies enhances the comparability and interpretability of our results within the broader literature.

Furthermore, approximately 40% of the MASALA study participants identified as vegetarians with limited consumption of red or processed meats.27 This characteristic may have increased the total PHDI scores since participants received higher scores for their restricted intake of the negatively scored animal proteins. In addition, it’s worth noting that while the MASALA cohort provided a valuable representation of the US South Asian population, it is not a nationally representative sample, thus limiting its generalizability. Efforts are underway to diversify the South Asian participant pool with additional recruitment of Bangladeshi and Pakistani individuals.76 Moreover, the use of an FFQ for ascertainment of dietary intake is subject to a certain degree of recall bias as well as measurement error.77 However, these are presumably nondifferential since the FFQ used by the MASALA study has been previously validated and captures foods unique to the South Asian diet.23,27

## CONCLUSIONS

This study demonstrated the validity and reliability of the PHDI developed in a South Asian population to measure adherence to the planetary health dietary guidelines set forth by the EAT-Lancet Commission. The PHDI exhibited similarities with the AHEI and was also associated with environmental benefits underscored by a lower dietary carbon footprint, emphasizing its broader focus on health and environmental sustainability. Future studies will aim to assess the predictive criteria of this index by examining the associations of the PHDI with specific health and disease outcomes in South Asian populations, contributing to our understanding of dietary patterns in relation to individual and planetary health.
